entities.name: Mateo de Toro Zambrano, 1st Count of La Conquista
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Mateo de Toro Zambrano y Ureta, 1st Count of La Conquista, was a pivotal figure in the late colonial history of Chile, serving as the last royal governor and the first president of the Government Junta of Chile in 1810. Born into a wealthy Criollo family in Santiago, his career spanned military service, administrative roles, and the accumulation of significant landholdings, solidifying his position within the Chilean aristocracy during the twilight of Spanish rule. His unexpected leadership of the initial independence movement, despite his deep loyalty to the Spanish crown, marks him as a complex and transitional figure at the dawn of a new era for South America.

Elevated to the 1st Count of La Conquista in 1770 by King Charles III, Toro Zambrano's influence grew through his extensive land ownership and his role as a knight of the Order of Santiago. In July 1810, at the age of 83, he was appointed Royal Governor of Chile following the deposition of Francisco Antonio García Carrasco. The political vacuum created by Napoleon's invasion of Spain and the subsequent abdication of Ferdinand VII led to immense pressure for self-governance. On September 18, 1810, Toro Zambrano presided over the open cabildo that established the First Government Junta of Chile, effectively initiating the Chilean War of Independence, though he himself remained a staunch monarchist.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Mateo de Toro Zambrano's reluctant leadership of the First Government Junta in 1810 was the crucial initial step in Chile's independence process, lending legitimacy to the movement and enabling the eventual formation of a national congress. His actions, despite his personal loyalties, directly triggered the end of Spanish colonial rule in Chile.
